As planned the reclamation and management of mined lands probably could produce wildlife with the abundance and diversity of the premining period, and it may be possible to increase numbers of desired species by habitat manipulation during reclamation.
Socio-Economic Effects
The local people, primarily the Crow Indians, can expect to go through some major changes in their way of life or contemporary culture. Whether these changes are desirable or undesirable, depends on local action and personal point of view.
Along with more jobs, labor income of both Crow and non-Crow is expected to rise substantially. Together with local expenditures by industry, and induced service businesses the net result will be a major increase in area income.
In the short-term, all local services will be overloaded. Service facilities including schools, health centers, utilities, and transportation systems will be overtaxed. In the short-term, all of this overload will create hardships on the Crow Indian people and other residents of the coal resource area. However, as facilities become adequate for the increased population, a greater number and variety of services should be available than were prior to coal development.
Permanent loss of existing scenic values and some archaeological sites of limited significance will occur because of disruption of the surface by the mining operation. Excavation will permit archaeological exploration that otherwise may never have been accomplished.
